analysis.one_liner: Tightens community-benefit rules that nonprofit hospitals must meet to keep their tax exemptions.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced with no cosponsors, it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the rest of the Congress and ended in a subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: Hospitals with nonprofit status skip federal, state, and local taxes — worth billions of dollars a year — on the theory that they give back to their communities. This bill would have tightened what they must do to keep that deal: they would have to spend at least as much on training, facilities, and free or discounted care as the value of their tax breaks; serve Medicare and Medicaid patients without turning them away; draw their boards from the local community; bill patients who qualify for charity care at Medicare rates instead of full charges; and face government reviews of how well they follow their own financial-assistance policies.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients served by tax-exempt hospitals, especially low-income and uninsured patients: the bill would require nonprofit hospitals to give more free and discounted care, cap what charity-care patients are billed at Medicare rates, and bar hospitals from limiting how many public-program patients they accept. Communities gain too, through required community-based boards and spending on facilities and training. Taxpayers benefit indirectly, because the bill ties a hospital's tax break to spending of equal value.

how_it_helps.text: Requires tax-exempt hospital organizations to spend at least 100% of the value of their federal, state, and local tax exemptions each year on patient-care training, facility and equipment improvements, and free or discounted care, with no more than half of the requirement met by facilities spending and purchases of other care-delivery businesses not counted at all.
Bars nonprofit hospitals from limiting the number of Medicare and Medicaid patients they serve at any clinical site they own or control, and requires them to treat public-program patients at all.
Requires that financial assistance (charity care) be billed at Medicare rates rather than full charges, limiting how much a qualifying patient can be charged for care.

Requires hospital boards to be drawn from the community where the hospital is located, and directs the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration and the Government Accountability Office to review and report on hospitals' financial-assistance policies and IRS enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt hospital organizations bear the cost: the spending requirement is sized to their entire tax-exemption value, charity-care billing at Medicare rates cuts their revenue from unpaid bills, and hospitals that fail to comply lose their 501(c)(3) exemption. Some of that cost could eventually be passed to paying patients or communities through facility closures or reduced services if hospitals cannot absorb it.

drawbacks.text: The spending threshold is set at 100% of the value of the hospital's tax exemptions, a figure that is hard to measure precisely and that a hospital could meet with spending it would do anyway, or — if it cannot — could push it toward giving up nonprofit status, which could change what services a community's hospital provides.

Capping financial-assistance billing at Medicare rates reduces revenue hospitals say they use to cross-subsidize care, and stricter requirements could add compliance costs or, in the worst case, contribute to service reductions in communities dependent on a single nonprofit hospital.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real but modest in design: the bill takes a widely criticized bargain — nonprofit hospitals collecting large tax breaks while some sue low-income patients and skimp on charity care — and attaches hard spending and patient-access conditions to the exemption. The costs fall on hospital balance sheets, not directly on taxpayers, and hospitals that cannot meet the standard would lose a privilege, not a mandate to operate. The main design risk is measurement: computing a hospital's total exemption value each year is difficult, and a rigid 100% floor could be gamed or could push marginal hospitals out of nonprofit status. On balance, the public benefit plausibly outweighs the cost, but the mechanism is blunt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with zero cosponsors, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and after a year and a half was sent to its Health subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the bill on April 25, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor during the entire two-year Congress.

The committee took no recorded action until December 17, 2024, near the end of the Congress, when the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tax-exempt hospitals are better off: they keep their existing community-benefit obligations and their tax exemptions unchanged, with no new spending floor, charity-care billing cap, or government reviews. Patients are left with the status quo rules.

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in Congress; no member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax exemption and hospital rules
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a hearing or markup in nearly two years; its only action was a routine referral to the Health subcommittee in the final weeks of the Congress.

against.name: Hospital industry associations
against.what_they_did: The nonprofit hospital sector has long opposed stricter community-benefit spending mandates and charity-care billing caps of this kind, arguing they threaten hospital finances; no association is recorded as taking a position on this specific bill, which died without gaining cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no party split is on record; the sole sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: Tax exemption is worth billions annually to the sector; the bill conditions it on community-benefit spending equal to the exemption's full value, bans limits on Medicare/Medicaid patients, caps charity-care bills at Medicare rates, and subjects hospitals to new oversight. Nonprofit hospitals profit from their tax status while some pursue low-income patients for full charges, so the sector's interest in this bill runs against patients and taxpayers.

industries.industry: For-profit hospital operators and practice acquirers
industries.note: The bill bars nonprofits from counting acquisitions of hospitals, physician practices, and other care-delivery organizations toward their community-benefit spending — a constraint aimed at the sector's consolidation strategy. For-profit acquirers are not directly regulated, but slowed nonprofit M&A could reduce acquisition opportunities for them.
